svg.text: How the cloud really moves one request
Your EC2 calls api.github.com. Follow the columns: what you configure → the hardware that does it → which network layer each place touches.
idea, not a place: it lives
in your view: ONE hop, straight to the NAT
switches, cables, spine: NOT in your view
no console page, nothing to configure
one NAT = a slice of a
one fiber path · the light travels this way →
The OSI model: a packet is built in layers, like nested envelopes. Each place opens only the layers it needs.
ZOOM INTO THE FIBER · L3 meets L1: the address, literally
Decimal is for humans. Machines see 32 bits. On the fiber, 1 = a flash of laser light, 0 = dark.
At 100 Gb/s that's 100 billion flashes a second: a whole packet passes in ~0.12 µs.

text.tspan: (L1, a hole in metal) picks the cable

svg.text: How the cloud pulls this off
One server hosts many customers. The AWS envelope carries the
VPC ID, so two VMs with the same IP never get mixed up.
Config up top, enforcement down below.
You edit config (the control plane). Nitro cards and Hyperplane
enforce it on every packet (the data plane). No cable moves.
NAT, IGW, the spine: all fleets of machines. They scale and
survive failures; a NAT and its subnet stay in one AZ.
Simplified from public AWS material (Nitro, Hyperplane, the VPC mapping service). Hosts, sockets and node numbers are illustrative.
